title: Paul's Defense on the Temple Steps
summary: Speaking in Hebrew from the steps of the Roman barracks, Paul tells the crowd how he was a zealous Pharisee trained under Gamaliel, persecuted the Way, met the risen Jesus on the road to Damascus, and was sent by him to the Gentiles. At the word Gentiles the crowd erupts again, and the commander orders Paul to be flogged and questioned. Paul reveals that he is a Roman citizen by birth, the flogging is stopped, and the commander summons the Sanhedrin to learn the charge against him.
story: Paul's arrest in chapter 21 leads to the first of five defense speeches that fill the last part of Acts. This is also the second of three tellings of his conversion (chapters 9, 22, and 26), each shaped for its audience. Here Paul speaks to a Jewish crowd that believes he has betrayed Israel, the law, and the temple, so he stresses everything that bound him to them: his upbringing in Jerusalem, his training in the law, his zeal, and the devout Jew Ananias. The speech is going well until it reaches the one claim the crowd cannot accept, that God sent him to the Gentiles. The chapter then shows Paul's Roman citizenship becoming the means by which he survives and, eventually, reaches Rome.
historical:
Gamaliel, under whom Paul says he studied, was a leading Pharisee and member of the Sanhedrin who counseled restraint toward the apostles in Acts 5:34-39. Later Jewish tradition remembers him as Rabban Gamaliel the Elder, a highly honored teacher, and describes him as the grandson of the great teacher Hillel, though that link comes from later sources. Paul's claim places him at the heart of Pharisaic learning in Jerusalem.

The scene turns on Roman citizenship. Citizens had legal protections that others lacked, including freedom from flogging without trial and the right to appeal to the emperor. The commander bought his citizenship at a high price, which fits reports that under Claudius citizenship could be obtained through bribes to officials; his name, Claudius Lysias (23:26), suggests he took the emperor's family name when he became a citizen, as new citizens often did. Paul, by contrast, was born a citizen, which means his father or an earlier ancestor held citizenship, perhaps granted for service to Rome. How a Jewish family in Tarsus obtained it is not known. Falsely claiming citizenship was a serious crime, which is why the commander accepts Paul's word and is alarmed at having chained him. The Sanhedrin was the Jewish high council in Jerusalem, led by the high priest, which Rome allowed to govern many internal matters.
cultural:
The Hebrew in which Paul speaks (verse 2) was probably Aramaic, the everyday language of Judea, though the term can also mean Hebrew proper. Choosing it rather than Greek signaled that he was one of them, and the crowd grows quieter. His opening, Brothers and fathers, is the same respectful address Stephen used before the Council (7:2). The crowd's reaction in verse 23, throwing off cloaks and tossing dust into the air, expressed outrage and perhaps a symbolic readiness to stone him.

The flogging the commander orders was not the beating with rods Paul suffered at Philippi, nor the Jewish penalty of forty lashes less one (2 Corinthians 11:24), but a Roman scourging with a whip of leather thongs, sometimes weighted with bone or metal, used to extract confessions from non-citizens. It could cripple or kill. Paul waits until he is being strapped down to ask his question, which makes the officers' danger all the greater. For Paul's Jewish hearers, the idea that God would send a faithful Jew away to the Gentiles implied that Israel's privileges were being shared with outsiders, and that, rather than Paul's faith in Jesus alone, is what triggers the riot.
literary: The speech is a formal defense (apologia, verse 1) built in three stages: Paul's former life (verses 3-5), his encounter with Jesus near Damascus (verses 6-16), and his vision in the temple (verses 17-21). Compared with chapter 9, Paul emphasizes Ananias's standing as a devout observer of the law, calls Jesus the Righteous One, and adds the temple vision, in which the Lord sends him to the Gentiles while he is praying in Israel's holiest place. The effect is to show that his mission to the Gentiles did not come from contempt for the temple but from the God of our fathers meeting him there. The chapter then shifts from speech to action, and the scene of the flogging is told with dramatic delay, the key fact held back until the last moment.

outline.t: The light and the voice near Damascus
The temple vision: sent to the Gentiles

doctrines.note: Ananias tells Paul, Get up, be baptized, and wash your sins away, calling on His name (verse 16). Forgiveness comes through calling on the name of Jesus, and baptism is its outward sign. Christians differ on how closely baptism and cleansing are joined, but all see here a new beginning received from Christ.

The Lord says, I will send you far away to the Gentiles. The mission that the crowd hears as betrayal is presented as the will of the God of our fathers, who always intended his blessing for the nations.
Paul's citizenship, an accident of birth, becomes the means by which God protects him and eventually brings him to Rome. God works through legal systems and circumstances as well as visions.

words.note: Apologia, a defense, the reasoned answer given in court, and the source of the English word apologetics. Paul begins, listen now to my defense. Peter later urges all believers to be ready to give such a defense of their hope (1 Peter 3:15).

Dikaios, righteous or just. Ananias calls Jesus the Righteous One, a title also used by Peter (3:14) and Stephen (7:52). It declares that the man condemned by Jerusalem's leaders was the one truly in the right before God.

Politeia, citizenship, the legal status of a citizen, and more broadly a way of life in a community. The commander bought his; Paul was born with his. Paul uses the same word in Ephesians 2:12 for the commonwealth of Israel, from which Gentiles had been excluded until Christ made them fellow citizens with the saints (Ephesians 2:19).
Apolouo, to wash off or wash away. It appears only here and in 1 Corinthians 6:11. The image connects baptism with cleansing from sin, the outward washing picturing an inward one.

christ: The heart of Paul's defense is that Jesus of Nazareth appeared to him and spoke to him. The risen Jesus identifies himself with his persecuted people (why do you persecute Me), so that harming them is harming him. Ananias calls him the Righteous One and says Paul was appointed to see him and hear his voice, which is what made Paul an apostle and witness. And in the temple, the place where Israel met its God, it is the Lord Jesus who appears and sends Paul to the nations. Paul presents his whole life as the result of being met, stopped, and redirected by the living Christ.

hard.q: Did Paul's companions hear the voice or not? Acts 9:7 and 22:9 seem to disagree.
hard.a:
In 9:7, Paul's companions stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one. In 22:9, Paul says his companions saw the light but could not understand the voice of the One speaking to me. On the surface one account says they heard and the other that they did not.

The usual explanation rests on the Greek verb akouo, which can mean to hear a sound or to hear with understanding. Many translations, including the BSB, render 22:9 as did not understand, reading the two accounts as saying that the companions heard a sound but did not make out the words, which were meant for Paul. Some grammarians also point to a difference in the case of the noun voice after the verb in the two passages, though others think that distinction is too fine to bear much weight. A third observation is that Luke, who wrote both accounts, evidently did not see a contradiction; he was content to tell the story differently for different audiences. Either way, both accounts agree that the experience was public and objective (others saw and heard something), but that its meaning was given to Paul alone.

questions: Paul began his defense by stressing everything he shared with his hearers. How can you speak about your faith in ways that begin from common ground?
The crowd listened until Paul mentioned the Gentiles. What word or idea about God's grace do people today find hardest to accept?
Paul used his Roman citizenship to protect himself. When is it right for a Christian to claim legal rights, and when might it be right to give them up?
